verdict_summary: 27 difference rows across the three units (10 grabber, 8 grabber_test, 9 websearch): rulebook right 23, native right 1, both defensible 3, both wrong 0. Both outputs are ruff-formatted (verified with the venv's ruff: 6 files already formatted) — no style discounts applied. The verdict distribution is lopsided toward the rulebook because B is a native baseline, not a parity attempt: it re-introduces two sanctioned fixes as bugs (FF-2 hardcoded limit, FF-4 unpinned UA), invents the tool name/description, uses the banned MCPServer+pydantic layer, and diverges from Go on regex anchors (trailing-newline URLs route to the API), host-case/port matching, 2xx handling, and byte-exact error strings. The rulebook won every one of those on Go-observable or judge-pinned evidence — those wins indict nothing. The single native-right row (urlsplit ValueError guard) and the three both-defensible rows (handler composition, structured/text block shape, month_year naming) are where the rulebook/inventory had no answer. 7 amendment-queue entries: 1 native-right consequence (row 29 ValueError guard), 1 SDK-behavior correction (row 91 bare-raise primary is wrong for mcp 2.3.0), 1 stale §1 API citation, 1 undecided multi-tool composition, 1 §2 pinned-string omission, 1 §2 test-rationale correction (rows 33/39 header-merge scope), 1 §4 naming case-split. FIVE of the seven touch sections/rows amended in round 1 (§1, §2 error row, §4 naming, github-grabber row 29, test rows 33/39) — each flagged in its entry; that concentration is itself a stop-signal datum for the human. Two process observations outside the queue: A's units import sibling modules that exist in neither workspace (the round-1 DEV-006 pattern recurring — A's code cannot import until the manifest's other units land, so its trailers' confidence=high is unverifiable in-workspace), and B silently exercised the banned MCPServer path while §1's decorator wording gave it cover — the cheapest fix is the queued §1 wording correction.
